title: Okra and Seafood Stew with Fish Sauce
author: Saveur
desc: Okra simmered in fish stock until it falls apart, enriched with palm oil and fish sauce, and finished with mussels and shrimp in the last four minutes.
longDesc: Where the Afrik soupou kandia leans on dried and fermented seafood, the Saveur one swaps in commercial fish sauce for every fermented ingredient and builds a clean, silky okra broth. Twelve cups of fish or vegetable stock are cooked with sliced okra, bay and onion about an hour and a half, until the okra is very tender and the stock has reduced by a quarter. Palm oil, fish sauce, aubergine and halved chiles go in for another 30 minutes, until the soup has thickened and the okra falls apart. Mussels and shrimp cook covered for about four minutes, until the mussels open, and the rest of the fish sauce is stirred in off the heat.
ingredients: 4 tbsp fish sauce, divided — 3 tbsp early, remainder off the heat
1 large eggplant, cut into large chunks, or 4 small Thai eggplants
2 habanero or Scotch bonnet chiles, slit in half lengthwise
Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
Cooked white rice or fonio, for serving
steps: Bring the stock to a boil in a 6-quart saucepan over high heat. Add the okra, bay leaves and onions, reduce to medium-low, and cook, stirring occasionally, until the okra is very tender and the stock has reduced by one-quarter — about 1 1/2 hours.
Add the palm oil, 3 tablespoons of the fish sauce, the eggplant and chiles. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the soup has thickened and the okra falls apart — about 30 minutes.
Add the mussels and shrimp, cover, and cook until the mussels open and the shrimp are cooked through — about 4 minutes. Discard any mussels that stay shut.
Remove from the heat. Stir in the remaining fish sauce and the pepper.
Ladle into bowls and serve with rice or fonio.
chefTips: The cues are ‘stock reduced by one-quarter’ and ‘okra falls apart’; both are visible and both beat the clock.
Hold back part of the fish sauce and stir it in off the heat — it keeps a fresher, sharper edge.
Discard any mussel that has not opened by the end of the four minutes.
Prick or split the chiles rather than chopping them if you want the heat in the broth but not in every bite.
commonMistakes: Adding mussels early so they toughen.
Stirring in all the fish sauce at the start.
reheating: Gentle heat, just to hot, so the shellfish do not toughen.
healthBenefits: Okra and aubergine give soluble fibre.
Mussels are a strong source of B12, iron and zinc.
culturalNote: The headnote calls this ‘undoubtedly a predecessor of Louisiana-style gumbo’. That is Saveur’s assertion, stated with no citation; it is recorded as a claim, not a fact. Compare SEN026, built on dried and fermented seafood, which is a materially different dish under the same name.
sources: Title as printed: ‘Okra and Seafood Stew (Soupoukandia)’. BYLINE: NONE PRINTED for the recipe. The page credits the photographer, Joseph De Leo; the parent article is credited in the headnote to John O’Connor. Organisation attribution: Saveur. DATE: none visible on the page; metadata gives 2012-04-19; the headnote says the recipe first appeared in the May 2012 issue. All three recorded. Yield: ‘serves 6-8’ (7 used here). TWO-PASS; no disagreement.
Times and cues in short fragments: ‘about 1 ½ hours’ with ‘stock has reduced by one-quarter’; ‘about 30 minutes’ with ‘okra falls apart’; ‘about 4 minutes’ with ‘mussels open’.

FERMENTATION: no guedj, yeet or nététou — the words appear nowhere on the page. Commercial fish sauce is the only fermented product; its split (3 tbsp early, remainder off the heat) is SINGLE-PASS from pass two. The remainder is derivable as 1 tbsp but is not printed as such.
The ingredient list prints ‘2 medium yellow onion’ (singular after a plural number) — as printed.

MAJOR DISAGREEMENT with SEN026, unreconciled: Afrik uses yet, nététou, dried and smoked fish, meat, crab and shrimp on a nokoss paste, puréed okra and few times; Saveur uses fish sauce in place of all fermented ingredients, no meat, mussels, simmered okra, and a time-driven method. Two materially different dishes; do not merge.
